item.description: <p><img src="../../ci-img/2026-08-20_nation-adjuncts.jpeg" width="auto" height="auto" alt=""></p> <p><a href="https://www.thenation.com/article/society/adjuncting-until-the-end-of-time/" class="external">Stories like this<svg aria-hidden="true" class="external-icon" style="max-width:0.8em;max-height:0.8em" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M320 0H288V64h32 82.7L201.4 265.4 178.7 288 224 333.3l22.6-22.6L448 109.3V192v32h64V192 32 0H480 320zM32 32H0V64 480v32H32 456h32V480 352 320H424v32 96H64V96h96 32V32H160 32z"></path></svg></a> have been a dime a dozen for decades, but I’d have to stretch my mind to think of <em>any</em> I’ve read that consider one of the most significant factors driving this trend: the expansion of practical degrees across higher ed. In many of those “new” fields and programs, expertise and relevance are established through practice across the field rather than research within the institution — so, for many purposes, adjuncts are often <em>preferable</em> to full-time faculty. And that assumes there even <em>are</em> qualified candidates for FT jobs. And that, in turn, raises the question of what “qualified” means: traditional academic credentials like a PhD? Some other terminal degree like an MFA or MS? (It’s only very recently that degrees like that have been accepted as legit grounds for FT jobs, let alone <em>tenure-track</em> jobs.) So, basically, the normative assumption driving pretty much all coverage of this subject over the last 25 years is that “traditional” faculty jobs in the humanities and social sciences are the notional baseline — even as those sectors have been shrinking in both absolute and relative terms. None of what I say here is a generic defense of higher ed’s turn toward mass-adjunctification. To be clear, much of it is abusive and I don’t support it. But the sad fact is that ostensibly critical coverage of this issue is basically a highbrow version of tradwife rhetoric: rooted in dying worlds, and waxing nostalgic for visions of it that never actually existed to begin with. But you won’t hear academics say any of this, because…well, now, <em>that</em> is an interesting question.</p>

item.description: <p>Ehud Olmert in Haartez: <a href="https://www.haaretz.com/opinion/2026-06-18/ty-article-opinion/.premium/israel-is-conducting-a-systematic-campaign-of-ethnic-cleansing-in-the-west-bank/0000019e-db02-d7a4-a99f-dfce00a20000" class="external">Israel Is Conducting a Systematic Campaign of Ethnic Cleansing and Crimes Against Humanity in the West Bank<svg aria-hidden="true" class="external-icon" style="max-width:0.8em;max-height:0.8em" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M320 0H288V64h32 82.7L201.4 265.4 178.7 288 224 333.3l22.6-22.6L448 109.3V192v32h64V192 32 0H480 320zM32 32H0V64 480v32H32 456h32V480 352 320H424v32 96H64V96h96 32V32H160 32z"></path></svg></a></p> <p>Lots of people will share piece this and shout <em>SEE?!?!? SEE?!?!</em>, but they shouldn’t, because it’s a tapestry woven from a dozen kinds of ambivalence. My read: OT1H, Olmert is working through the five stages of grief; OT2H, he’s trying to chart a new and better course — not just for himself — in a context where everyone who politically matters can be assessed on a scale that runs from directly complicit to guilty ‘af.’ If you read his essay that way, as an exploratory rather than confirmatory text, you’ll see that the majority of it is devoted to a scholastic exercise in finding guilt without assigning it. Why? Because he’s trying to give a crazy quilt of conflicting constituencies face-saving ways to moonwalk out of the corner Israel has painted itself into. That’s a Good Thing, and if your political beliefs are so “absolute” that you can’t acknowledge it as such, then you live in a fantasy land and have no business imposing your views on a world where nothing is ever absolute.</p>

item.description: <p>[Orig to <a href="https://www.facebook.com/tbyfield/posts/pfbid0P3KTFDfJrpmYDeNisxF3Rwebw6TA1hwAhpDyfJzTECu9b9p3LBTpvTzB9jDpWUHnl" class="external">FB<svg aria-hidden="true" class="external-icon" style="max-width:0.8em;max-height:0.8em" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M320 0H288V64h32 82.7L201.4 265.4 178.7 288 224 333.3l22.6-22.6L448 109.3V192v32h64V192 32 0H480 320zM32 32H0V64 480v32H32 456h32V480 352 320H424v32 96H64V96h96 32V32H160 32z"></path></svg></a>]</p> <p>In the run-up to the last presidential election, it was my strong sense that Netanyahu’s government was carefully modulating its war effort specifiucally to stoke conflict among US Dems / libs / progs / lefts. Put plainly, in my view, he used ethnic cleansing and genocide as a lever to <em>punk</em> the US ‘left’ into the internecine warfare that contributed to Trump’s election. I think that’s happening again this election season, with the aim of minimizing the risk that the Dems win both houses. Netanyahu himself can’t be seen as doing this right when Trump is ripping him a new one over the phone, so instead we saw (1) an astonishingly large group of ultra cabinet ministers and Knessest members at NYC’s Israel Day parade, (2) ginned-up media outrage over Mamdani’s principled choice not to attend, and (3) low-level background noise about whether this or that US politician knew in advance which genocidal lunatics would be out in front — all signs of a state visit without all the statery. The implication of this view is that Israel’s ultra-aggressive incursions into Lebanon are driven in part, possibly in large part, by their political reception in the US: the worse the reception here, the better for Israeli fascists. If so, ideas about “complicity” that have been so faddish on the left for the last few years, are mostly backwards: the louder you yell GENOCIDE, the more likely Netanyahu and Crew are to actually do it. They want to do it anyway, they benefit from the collapse of the civility that makes debate possible, they kneecap the universities they see as factories of anti-Israel sentiment, and they hobble the left-leaning segments of the Democratic Party.</p>

item.description: <p>[Orig to <a href="https://www.facebook.com/tbyfield/posts/pfbid02bUXNR1Sko5J23qTGGWe5EbBdM2KHynyFQyETEXm3i5FyUtfCadAxsyp338zYJvuKl" class="external">FB<svg aria-hidden="true" class="external-icon" style="max-width:0.8em;max-height:0.8em" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M320 0H288V64h32 82.7L201.4 265.4 178.7 288 224 333.3l22.6-22.6L448 109.3V192v32h64V192 32 0H480 320zM32 32H0V64 480v32H32 456h32V480 352 320H424v32 96H64V96h96 32V32H160 32z"></path></svg></a>]</p> <p>This “<a href="https://president.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2026-04/Report-of-the-Committee-on-Trust-in-Higher-Education.pdf" class="external">Report of the Yale Committee on Trust in Higher Education<svg aria-hidden="true" class="external-icon" style="max-width:0.8em;max-height:0.8em" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M320 0H288V64h32 82.7L201.4 265.4 178.7 288 224 333.3l22.6-22.6L448 109.3V192v32h64V192 32 0H480 320zM32 32H0V64 480v32H32 456h32V480 352 320H424v32 96H64V96h96 32V32H160 32z"></path></svg></a>” is worth reading, or a least a serious skim. The committee that drafted it was given an impossible task, and it shows. There’s a <em>lot</em> of slippery rhetoric in it — for example, “Families want to know why college costs so much and why costs keep rising. Economists have identified a variety of structural factors, including the labor-intensive nature of education, the need for competitive salaries to attract skilled professionals, and the flow of federal student aid. In public discourse, the most common critiques point to administrative bloat, spending on buildings, and the ‘corporatization’ of the university. Opinion polls show widespread suspicion that colleges and universities, like other businesses, are primarily out to make a profit—though most are, legally speaking, not-for-profit institutions.” That’s the only substantive mention of real estate development, which is a major culprit in distorting and distracting from “the mission.” And the larger criticism isn’t the “corporatization” of higher ed, it’s the <em>financialization</em> — which that last bit tiptoes around. The recommendations (p. 23ff.) aren’t bad, though they’re awfully vague. #9, “Open the gates,” is a good one and it mirrors what I told the New School back when I chaired the faculty senate: The cost of running university in an urban core is <em>guaranteed</em> to skyrocket, making it entirely dependent on catering to the wealthy. The only alternatives were either (1) move the entire school somewhere cheaper, or (2) fundamentally rethink its relationship to the city at different scales — by opening up to it. Instead, they blew multiples of the university endowment on an lavish architectural white elephant, then elevated the person who was largely responsible for guiding that to the presidency, where most of his time is spent frantically trying to keep it from going bust. But urban schools are just a bleeding edge of a growing massacre in US higher ed.</p>

item.title: 2026-04-06-the fog of war is very thick

The fantasy of war with China
item.description: <p>[Orig to <a href="https://www.facebook.com/tbyfield/posts/pfbid0PGBu1j8gpbzjUneZNoat3BjBwFHReg3t7fGL8X2wbgXeMY7tztJT2UKu7tY4PVFgl" class="external">FB<svg aria-hidden="true" class="external-icon" style="max-width:0.8em;max-height:0.8em" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M320 0H288V64h32 82.7L201.4 265.4 178.7 288 224 333.3l22.6-22.6L448 109.3V192v32h64V192 32 0H480 320zM32 32H0V64 480v32H32 456h32V480 352 320H424v32 96H64V96h96 32V32H160 32z"></path></svg></a>]</p> <p>The idea that the US ever would or could fight an actual, serious war against China is a quaint delusion, barely one step above Trump’s senescent fantasy that we can just “take” Iran’s oil. What, the US is going to send its big mean Navy across the Pacific to bomb Beijing into submission? Or are we going to send our boys over there to invade — you know, enough “boots on the ground” to occupy Shanghai (22M people), Beijing (19M), Shenzhen (18M), Guangzhou (16M), Chengdu (14M), Tianjin (11M), Wuhan (11M), Donguan (10M), Chongqing (10), Xi’an (9M), Hangzhou (9M), and all the other millions needed to make 1.4 BILLION people? And they’ll be supported by a country where every single thing, from the smallest screw to the most immense prefab construction module, is literally <em>made in China</em>? If the PRC pulled the plug on even a tiny fraction of its business with the US — financial, material, technical, logistical, and of course human — the entire country would collapse without the slightest hope of rebuilding. Ever. Amazon? Crickets. The big-box stores that killed off entire categories of mom-and-pops across the country? Shelves empty. Got a vehicle, an appliance, a computer, a machine, a device, a gizmo, or a system <em>of any kind</em> that breaks? You’ll never fix it, so it’s only value will be cannibalizing it for parts. Food? Enjoy waiting in line for whatever’s available, because countless ingredients needed for industrial-scale food prep in factories and restaurants will run out. And it’s not just this or that system or thing breaking — the repercussions of <em>every</em> failure would ripple out and cascade across every aspect of life at every scale. But you’ll never hear anyone say any of this. Quite the opposite: Serious People love to speculate about the coming war with China, and speculating about the coming war with China is a sign that you’re a Serious Person.</p>
